title: The Sunday Bus
direction: On her last afternoon at the library, Helen emptied the drawer everyone had always called hers.
notes: About four and three-quarter minutes, in fifteen shots, drawn in code on a canvas with the same approach as the other two films, and paced so every caption can be read. The Mondays at the library are a sepia memory, with the calendar flipping faster as the invitations stop; Martin's route and note write themselves onto the map in blue ink; at the chapel he returns only as an outline, his sayings in his handwriting and his speech balloon empty. Click the animation to pause it.

title: The Sunday Bus (read aloud)
direction: On her last afternoon at the library, Helen emptied the drawer everyone had always called hers.
notes: The Sunday Bus with a reader's voice: every caption is read aloud, and so are the title and Martin's note on the map. The voice is AI-generated (OpenAI gpt-4o-mini-tts, voice “fable”, asked for a British reader), made once with narrate.py and played from audio files. Each caption stays up until its line has been spoken, so the film runs a little longer than the silent one. Click to begin; the button at the top right turns the sound off and on.

title: O Autocarro de Domingo
direction: Na sua última tarde na biblioteca, a Helen esvaziou a gaveta a que todos sempre tinham chamado sua.
notes: The Portuguese (European) version of The Sunday Bus: captions and on-screen writing are in Portuguese, and it follows the translation's different ending, in which Helen turns the map over and finds the back blank. It can also be read aloud in European Portuguese: the narration is off at the start, and the button at the top right turns it on (an AI-generated voice, OpenAI “marin”). Click the animation to pause it.

title: Der Sonntagsbus
direction: Am letzten Nachmittag in der Bibliothek leerte Helen die Schublade, die alle immer ihre genannt hatten.
notes: The same film as The Sunday Bus, in German: captions, map labels, handwriting, signs and the title are all translated. About six and a half minutes, because the German captions use the slower reading pace (about 120 words a minute) and hold scenes rather than speed the action. Click the animation to pause it.

title: The Landing
direction: The building had six floors and a laundry room in the basement.
notes: About seven and a half minutes, in twenty shots, paced so every caption can be read. The story is long, so the film is an adaptation: it keeps the key moments and uses the story's own words for its captions, with some lines shortened or joined. The fourth-floor landing is the recurring set; objects carry the story (the washing machine that has to be told twice, the saucepan, the folder moved off a café chair, messages typed and deleted, the bookcase and its pale ring). The surnames on the nameplate are invented. Click the animation to pause it.

title: The Missing Tree
direction: The complaint arrived during the first hot week. Your shaded route has no shade.
notes: About four minutes, in thirteen shots, drawn in code on a canvas with the same approach as The Space Between Words. The map layers flip like drawings on a peg bar; the tablet shows the tree the forecast still believes in; at the end the spare umbrella's square of shade travels off with the woman. Captions are taken from the story, a few lines shortened. Click the animation to pause it.

title: The Space Between Words
direction: After the post-office fire, the surviving letters were taken to the schoolhouse. Two copyists sat at desks built for children.
notes: About two minutes, in ten shots, drawn in code on a canvas. Characters are animated on twos with boiling ink lines over still painted backgrounds, with multiplane parallax and narration captions taken from the story. Some exchanges (“Mine shows where we cannot read”) and the afternoon of revisions are left out for length. Click the animation to pause it.

title: Palavras que não cabem em inglês
direction: Little vignettes to illustrate words in Portuguese that have no simple English equivalent. Each animated scene will illustrate on of these words and explain in Portuguese what they mean and then list the English equivalent phrases.
notes: About three and a half minutes: six comic vignettes, one for each verb (caber, aproveitar, desabafar, madrugar, pernoitar, caprichar), with one recurring character, Zé. Each opens on the word, explains it in European Portuguese in the captions, and ends on a pinned card with English equivalents. The gags: a suitcase that fits the boot only if Zé sits on it; a hotel breakfast that was “already paid for”; a storm cloud that drains out of Zé and settles over his friend; Zé up so early he has to wake the rooster («Deus ajuda quem cedo madruga»); one night in a bed too short for him; a cake finished with ruler, spirit level and tweezers, until the cherry proves too much for the table. Captions use the slower reading pace for a second language. It can also be read aloud: the narration is off at the start, and the button at the top right turns it on (an AI-generated voice, OpenAI “marin”, reading the Portuguese in a European accent and the English cards in English with a light Portuguese accent). Click the animation to pause it.

title: The Sheep and the Horses
direction: Schleicher's fable (a vignette about the world of the Indo-Europeans). Animate it using an English text.
notes: About two minutes, in nine shots, drawn in code on a canvas with the same approach as the other films. August Schleicher's 1868 fable, written in his reconstruction of Proto-Indo-European, is told in English captions (a close translation of his own German gloss) and set on the steppe of the Indo-Europeans: feather grass, burial mounds on the horizon, a wagon with solid wheels, and stocky dun horses with upright manes. The horses' explanation is shown as a painted band turning round a pot: wool plucked, spun on a drop spindle, woven on a warp-weighted loom, and worn as a cloak. It ends with Schleicher's reconstructed text. Click the animation to pause it.

title: Room 4
direction: This animation is an alternate history of education in the United States at the grade school level from the 1960s to the present. In this version, television is used to replace printed texts and textbooks as far as possible. So, we want a series of 5 vignettes from 1960s to 2026 showing how this affects student work and progress. We see students in classrooms watching videos. Teachers in the classroom are now like tutors helping students individually. We see students working in their home watching videos. After the 1980s and 1990s especially, these videos are on computer screens and not on just television monitors.
notes: About four and three-quarter minutes, in seventeen shots and five vignettes (1962, 1975, 1988, 2004, 2026), drawn in code on a canvas with the same approach as the other films. It starts from a real experiment: from 1961 an airplane circled over Indiana broadcasting lessons to schools (the Midwest Program on Airborne Television Instruction). In this history the experiment never ended. One classroom, Room 4, is the recurring set: the same clock, closet and window, with a tree outside, planted in 1962, that grows through the decades. The lesson changes from a broadcast that cannot see the class, to a tape you can rewind, to a video that pauses for you, while the teacher moves from the front of the room to kneeling beside one child at a time. The two home scenes rhyme: in 1975 Linda misses the answer while her mother brings a snack (and turns the channel back with her toe), and in 2004 she brings her own son a snack and he presses pause. The costs are shown too: children who can explain photosynthesis but not spell it. It ends with the textbooks boxed up in 1962 being found again. The school, the teachers and the children are invented. Click the animation to pause it.

title: O Raio de Sol
direction: Um habitante do litoral português sentado na esplanada sob céu nublado avista um único raio de sol minúsculo que rompe as nuvens; corre desenfreado, arrasta a cadeira de praia em frações de segundo e estende-se exatamente naquele círculo de calor antes que ele desapareça.
notes: About seventy seconds, in nine shots, drawn in code on a canvas with the same approach as the other films. Almost wordless: the only words are the title, two captions in Portuguese (“Agosto.” and “Foi o verão.”) and a pharmacy cross showing 16°. A grey northern seafront: an azulejo-tiled café with wave-pattern pavement, rows of empty striped beach tents, a low ceiling of cloud. The run itself is too fast to draw, so it is a smear and a cloud of dust; his flat cap hangs in the air for a moment before it falls, and back at the café a gull eats his pastel de nata. In the light he finds his head is still in the shade and shuffles the chair over twice; when the circle shrinks he folds himself up to stay in it, and when it closes he stays anyway. The café and the town are invented. Click the animation to pause it.

title: Das Grimmsche Gesetz
direction: Das Grimmsche Gesetz – im Deutschen fachsprachlich als Erste Lautverschiebung bekannt – markiert den Moment, in dem sich das Urgermanische im 1. Jahrtausend v. Chr. als eigenständige Sprachfamilie aus dem Indoeuropäischen herausbildete.
notes: An animated lecture in German, about seven and a half minutes, at the slower reading pace for German captions. The text's suggested visuals become the drawings: Grimm at his desk beneath a fairy-tale picture beside the 1822 title page of the Deutsche Grammatik, a map of the Germanic core area around 750–500 BC, a musical-chairs game of sound creatures, gears, one mechanism for each phase (a blocked pipe, a voice wave going flat, a puff of breath), Grimm's closed circle, and the cognate matrix, ending with genu, dent- and ager to decode. Each sound class keeps one colour throughout. A few additions for accuracy: Latin is shown as a cognate ("entspricht"), not an ancestor; examples for phase 3 (bhrātar/brother, thýra/door); a note that Zahn, Herz and zehn also show the second, High German shift. The Grimm figure is a generic drawing, not a likeness. Click the animation to pause it.

title: VR, Film, and the Far Side of the Uncanny Valley
direction: An animated essay after the essay by Jay Bolter and Maria Engberg.
notes: About twenty minutes, in five chapters following the essay's sections. The essay (about 7,200 words) is distilled into roughly a third as many words of captions, mostly in its own phrasing, with concrete images where possible and diagrams where necessary: Mori's graph with a walker who falls into the valley, the Lumière train in a flinching theatre, the asymptote of film's resemblance to life, the La Ciotat myth and effect, Benjamin's fading aura, Freud's heimlich and unheimlich, the Body Snatchers pods, the doubles of Us, Todorov's hesitation, avatars, the Hawaii alert, codec-avatar busts, and the layered gap of VR embodiment. The codec avatars are generic figures, not likenesses. Click the animation to pause it.
